title: 'Proof' time travel is 'real' with unusual detail spotted in 1937 painting
excerpt: A painting created in 1937 by Umberto Romano shows a Native American man holding something very unexpected
content:
A painting created in 1937 by Umberto Romano shows a Native American man holding something very unexpected

07:00, 05 Sep 2026Updated 09:47, 05 Sep 2026

Conspiracy theorists are adamant that a nearly century-old artwork showing a Native American man clutching what looks like a 'mobile phone' proves time travel exists.

‌

The artwork, titled Mr Pynchon and the Settling of Springfield, was crafted by Italian artist Umberto Romano in 1937 and depicts settlers arriving in the town during the 1620s.

‌

A local figure can be seen wielding a small, dark rectangular item that resembles an iPhone, staring straight down at it, almost as though he's snapping a selfie.

‌

This peculiar item has baffled viewers, with many concluding it might suggest time travel, given that iPhones weren't created until 2007.

Nevertheless, Brian Anderson, writing for Motherboard, determined that the gadget is most probably a mirror.

‌

Mr Anderson explained: "There's reason to believe, then, that what the man is examining is not an Indigenous object, but rather of European origin, like mirrors, which were presented often in such exchanges," he wrote.

"The way the man holds it up, if indeed he's looking at his own face reflecting back at him, would certainly make sense."

‌

However, this isn't the first time of a 'mobile phone' being identified in artwork long before the gadget's creation.

Conspiracy theorists backed the time travel theory after a woman was spotted clutching a 'mobile phone' in the background of a Charlie Chaplin movie from 1928.

The black and white footage of the alleged 'time traveller' was taken from the comic's silent picture, The Circus. In the footage, a woman wearing a black top hat and white gloves can be spotted strolling in the background of the scene, clutching what looks like a gadget in her hand, with several viewers suggesting she's gripping a mobile phone.

‌

Portable mobile phones weren't commercially available until the 1980s, roughly 50 years following the Charlie Chaplin picture's debut. Irish director George Clarke discovered the 'time traveller' in the 1928 movie back in 2010 before posting his findings on his Youtube channel.

In the clip, which has now garnered almost seven million views, the director explained: "If you look carefully, she's talking on a thin, black device that is held to her ear. If you notice also that the knuckles are bent in the flat shape of a phone.

Article continues below

"The phone is to the ear. It's not an ear trumpet. It is not an AM/FM radio, obviously because it's 1928. Technically, there's nothing that can explain [what] is in her hand... It's clear she's talking. She's on her own. She's talking into the device."

Several days following George's Youtube upload, conspiracy theorists started sharing their theories about the 'time traveller' material. Some proposed that the woman was simply protecting her face from sunlight, while others argued she was holding her ear.

Nevertheless, the Daily News swiftly dismissed the conspiracies, declaring that "while this fantastical theory is fun to ponder, in all likelihood the woman is actually using a hearing aid."
